strengths: Principled Conceptual Framework: Adapting procedural generation principles to algorithm discovery benchmarks is a novel and timely contribution. In particular, enforcing a rigorous meta-train / meta-test separation (evaluating discovered algorithms on held-out datasets unknown to the agent during discovery) directly addresses a critical methodological deficiency in current ADA benchmarks.

Broad and Diverse ML Domains: The framework spans 14 diverse machine learning domains (including Bayesian optimization, continual learning, language modeling, unlearning, several RL paradigms, and trajectory prediction), providing broad coverage of typical ML engineering and research workflows.

Comprehensive Empirical Diagnostics: The paper goes beyond standard benchmark tables by conducting informative analyses, such as rank-correlation analysis between tasks (confirming low redundancy and semantic shift across splits), difficulty scaling over editable module count, and empty vs. baseline initializations.

Demonstrated Utility for Agent Optimization: The prompt-tuning experiments (Section 7) validate the central thesis that optimizing agents across a procedurally sampled distribution of tasks improves out-of-distribution generalization compared to optimizing on a single fixed task.

Thorough Documentation and Reproducibility: The submission provides extensive details in the appendix, including mathematical derivations of configuration spaces, dataset splits, full agent prompts, per-task metric breakdowns, and an open-source release.
weaknesses: Combinatorial Masking vs. True Procedural Content Generation: While claiming '~100B tasks', the vast majority of this space comes from combinatorial dataset subsetting ($3^d$) and module toggling ($2^m$) across 14 fixed code repositories and ~97 total base datasets. While practically useful, framing this purely as 'procedural generation' is somewhat overstated compared to procedural generation in RL (which programmatically synthesizes new dynamics, levels, or data distributions).

Agent Failure Modes Conflate Coding Robustness with Research Capability: In the more challenging configurations (e.g., 'All Edit'), agent success rates drop drastically (17.8% to 40.5%), with many failures resulting from syntax errors, wrong dimensions, or API mismatches. While this indicates substantial headroom, the evaluation frequently tests basic software scaffolding and type-checking rather than genuine algorithmic reasoning.

Limited Scope of Agent Optimization: The demonstration of ADA optimization is restricted to meta-prompt tuning over 30 iterations. While sensible given compute constraints, it remains a relatively modest realization of the broader vision outlined in Section 6 (e.g., policy fine-tuning, world models, or search-based self-improvement).

Underperformance Relative to Standard Baselines: Even in the 'Until Success' setting where crashes are excluded (Table 7), none of the evaluated open-weight LLMs consistently match or outperform the fixed standard baseline on meta-test, indicating that agents are currently struggling to produce net-positive algorithmic innovations systematically.

strengths: Compelling Problem Formulation: The paper clearly articulates critical failure modes in existing ADA (Algorithm Discovery Agent) benchmarks—most notably the confounding of discovery and evaluation sets (lack of meta-train/meta-test splits), risks of pretraining contamination, and severe sample limitations due to manual curation.

Broad and Modular Framework: DiscoGen provides a highly general, modular formulation spanning 14 diverse machine learning domains (from Bayesian optimization and neural cellular automata to offline RL and trajectory prediction). Combinatorially parameterizing editable modules, splits, and initializations yields a vast space of valid tasks (~100 billion).

Principled Evaluation Methodology (DiscoBench): By standardizing the 'Single Edit' vs. 'All Edit' paradigms and enforcing strict isolation of meta-test sets (preventing data leakage and code-injection hacks), the authors set a solid standard for benchmarking research agents.

Comprehensive Empirical Validation and Scaling Study: Beyond baseline model evaluations (DeepSeek-v3.2, Devstral2, GPT-OSS 120B), the automated prompt optimization experiments convincingly show that optimizing ADAs across an increasing number of procedurally generated tasks (K_tasks) translates to monotonic gains in meta-test generalization, both in-distribution and out-of-distribution.

Exemplary Depth and Transparency: The 116-page manuscript provides meticulous detail, including mathematical task derivations, Spearman rank correlation analyses proving cross-task diversity, compute cost breakdowns, complete system prompt evolutions, and per-task result distributions.
weaknesses: Limited Agent Architectural Diversity: The empirical evaluation exclusively utilizes a single agent scaffold (the ReAct-based MLGym agent). While evaluating different base LLMs is informative, testing diverse ADA architectures (such as tree-search, evolutionary code mutation, or reflection-heavy agents) would demonstrate how the benchmark differentiates various agentic strategies.

High Execution Failure Rates in Complex Tasks: In the 'All Edit' regime, success rates drop dramatically (17.8%–40.5%). Consequently, a substantial portion of the Elo ranking signal is driven by agents producing syntax errors or hardcoded shape mismatches rather than true differences in algorithmic design quality.

Restricted Scope of ADA Optimization: The optimization experiments demonstrate prompt tuning via an external LLM (Claude 3.5/4.5 Sonnet). While effective as a proof of concept, this leaves open questions about the feasibility and dynamics of gradient-based or RL-based agent fine-tuning on DiscoGen tasks.

strengths: Principled Task Formulation: The paper addresses a major structural flaw in existing automated machine learning / algorithm discovery benchmarks (e.g., MLE-bench, MLGym-Bench) by strictly enforcing a meta-train versus held-out meta-test split across datasets. This prevents agents from over-optimizing to specific evaluation data and measures true algorithmic generalization.

Scale and Domain Breadth: DiscoGen covers 14 distinct ML domains (ranging from Bayesian optimization and continual learning to multi-agent RL, offline RL, and LLM unlearning). Through modular configuration (editable vs. fixed components, dataset splits, backends), it enables procedural sampling across billions of task variations.

Demonstration of ADA Optimization: The authors demonstrate a concrete and compelling use case by optimizing agent prompts via an external meta-LLM across varying task budgets (Ktasks = 1, 5, 10, 30). The results convincingly show that training over a broader distribution of procedural tasks improves out-of-distribution generalization to held-out domains.

Comprehensive Empirical Analysis: The submission includes thorough analyses of task difficulty scaling (e.g., success rate vs. number of active editable modules), the impact of scaffold initialization (empty template vs. baseline implementation), rank correlation across tasks, and extensive per-task breakdown in the 116-page manuscript.
weaknesses: Combinatorial Inflation of Task Count: The claim of '~100 billion tasks' is driven by combinatorial combinations of dataset inclusion/exclusion and module toggles across 14 codebases. While mathematically valid, many generated tasks within the same domain are closely related variations rather than qualitatively distinct discovery challenges.

Floor Effects and Agent Failure Rates: Existing open-weight models struggle significantly on the multi-module discovery tasks (success rates of only 17.8% to 40.5% on DiscoBench All Edit) and fail to beat human-designed baseline implementations in aggregate Elo. While this demonstrates room for ADA development, high failure rates driven by syntax and tensor shape mismatches somewhat obscure algorithmic reasoning capability.

Limited Optimization Paradigm: The conceptual framing heavily emphasizes training generalist discovery agents via reinforcement learning or autocurricula, but the experimental evaluation is limited to prompt optimization via a proprietary LLM (Claude Sonnet 4.5). Demonstrating weight-level finetuning or direct RL on smaller open models would have strengthened the central claims.

Computational Cost for Benchmarking: While individual tasks can run on consumer GPUs, full evaluations and meta-optimization require substantial compute resources (estimated at 35,000 GPU-hours on Nvidia H200s in Appendix C.5), posing barriers for standard academic labs seeking to train ADAs over large curricula.

strengths: Conceptual framing: The paper makes a compelling case for applying procedural content generation (PCG) to algorithm discovery tasks, addressing critical flaws in existing ADA benchmarks such as data contamination, lack of clear meta-train/meta-test splits, and manual authoring bottlenecks.

Rigor and task design: Tasks are modularly structured across 10 diverse ML subfields (spanning BO, CV, RL, UED, and language modeling), enabling controlled experimental intervention on specific components (e.g., loss vs. optimizer vs. architecture) and distinct generalization evaluations.

Comprehensive empirical benchmarking: DiscoBench provides rigorous baseline evaluations with open-source LLMs (DeepSeek-V3.2, Devstral-2, GPT-OSS 120B), paired with detailed Elo ratings, bootstrap confidence intervals, success@k analysis, and task-to-task rank-correlation studies.

Demonstration of utility: The case study on prompt optimization demonstrates a clear monotonic relationship between the diversity of procedurally sampled tasks ($K_{tasks}$) and held-out meta-test generalization, empirically validating the benefit of procedural task generation for ADA development.

Thoroughness and reproducibility: The paper includes extensive documentation, derivations, environment descriptions, exact system prompts, and full task-level result breakdowns in the appendix, along with an open-source release.
weaknesses: Combinatorial inflation of task counts: The claim of >400 million (or ~100 billion in the appendix) tasks relies heavily on combinatorial subsets of a modest number of datasets ($3^d - 2^{d+1} + 1$) and editable module combinations ($2^m - 1$) across ~10 core base codebases, which can somewhat overstate the structural diversity of the task space.

High agent failure floor on multi-module tasks: In DiscoBench All, current frontier open-source agents achieve very low completion success rates (11.4%–34.3%), driven by syntax errors and shape mismatches, indicating that multi-module tasks currently suffer from a floor effect for off-the-shelf agents.

Limited meta-optimization scope: While Section 6 outlines exciting avenues (e.g., training algorithm world models, RL post-training of ADAs), the actual demonstration in Section 7 is restricted to prompt tuning via a closed-source LLM across up to 30 steps, leaving direct agent weight optimization or autocurricula as future work.

strengths: Principled framing of algorithm discovery: The paper addresses fundamental methodological weaknesses in existing ADA benchmarks (such as MLE-Bench and MLGymBench), specifically by strictly separating algorithm discovery (meta-train) from algorithm evaluation (meta-test) to measure transfer and generalization rather than dataset memorization.

Broad coverage across diverse ML subfields: DiscoGen integrates 10 distinct task domains spanning Bayesian optimization, computer vision, continual learning, language modeling, model unlearning, and reinforcement learning, each decomposed into modular, editable interfaces.

Empirical validation of task diversity and utility: The rank correlation analysis (Appendix I) convincingly shows that task performance is non-redundant and that agent rankings shift substantially between meta-train and meta-test splits. Furthermore, the prompt optimization experiment (Section 7, Table 3) provides concrete evidence that optimizing an agent across diverse procedurally generated tasks directly improves generalization on held-out test benchmarks.

Comprehensive documentation and experimental rigor: The submission is thorough, providing detailed task configurations, prompts, per-task breakdowns, bootstrapping methodology for Elo ratings, and extensive appendices analyzing module difficulty hierarchies.
weaknesses: Combinatorial vs. truly generative procedural generation: While the paper claims hundreds of millions of tasks, the task generator is essentially a combinatorial product over a modest pool of human-curated datasets, backends, and boolean module flags (Equation 1). It does not procedurally synthesize new mathematical formulations, environments, or code logic from scratch.

High execution failure rates dilute algorithmic evaluation in complex tasks: In DiscoBench All, agent success rates range between 11.4% and 34.3%, indicating that a large portion of the evaluation signal in challenging regimes reflects an LLM's inability to avoid syntax/interface errors rather than algorithm quality or research ingenuity.

Evaluation of agent optimization is limited to prompt tuning: Although the paper heavily motivates DiscoGen as an engine for training generalist research agents via RL, autocurricula, or meta-learning (Sections 1 and 6), the only realized demonstration of the ADA optimization loop is prompt search guided by Claude Sonnet over 30 steps.

Substantial computational requirements: Running end-to-end inner-loop training and meta-loop discovery requires significant compute (~23,000 GPU-hours reported across development and experiments), which somewhat contrasts with the paper's stated motivation of facilitating ADA development outside large industrial labs.

strengths: Principled Task Formulation: The paper addresses a major structural flaw in existing AI research agent benchmarks (such as MLE-bench and MLGym-Bench) by enforcing a strict separation between meta-training and meta-testing. This prevents agents from merely overfitting algorithms to the test datasets and directly evaluates out-of-distribution algorithm transfer.

Broad Domain Coverage and Modular Design: DiscoGen spans 10 distinct machine learning domains (including Bayesian optimization, continual learning, LLM unlearning, computer vision, and on/off-policy RL) with modular interfaces that allow selective editing of specific components (loss, architecture, optimizer, training loop). This provides a flexible sandbox for algorithmic innovation rather than brute-force codebase generation.

Comprehensive Diversity and Pathology Analysis: The paper provides thorough diagnostic analysis, including Spearman rank correlation matrices across tasks and between meta-train and meta-test splits (Figures 2 & 3). The rank shuffling between meta-train and meta-test provides empirical evidence against task redundancy and illustrates how algorithm rankings vary across datasets.

Validation via Meta-Optimization: The case study in Section 7 provides a concrete demonstration of using procedurally generated tasks for prompt optimization. Showing a monotonic improvement in meta-test performance on DiscoBench as the number of sampled training tasks increases (from K=1 to K=30) strongly validates the utility of procedural task diversity for training/tuning ADAs.

Exceptional Open-Source and Diagnostic Completeness: The manuscript and extensive appendices (128 pages) provide comprehensive documentation, complete prompt templates, per-task performance distributions, and full implementation specifications across all domains.
weaknesses: Combinatorial Scaling vs. Semantic Uniqueness: The claim of supporting >400 million (and up to ~100 billion) tasks is driven primarily by combinatorics of dataset partitioning ($3^d$) and module toggles ($2^m$). While mathematically sound and useful for preventing identical repeated tasks during meta-training, many generated tasks within the same domain are closely related variations rather than qualitatively distinct algorithmic challenges.

Narrow Agent Exploration: The benchmark evaluation focuses exclusively on a single agent scaffold (the ReAct agent from MLGym) paired with three open-weights LLMs. Evaluating alternative agent architectures (such as evolutionary search or MCTS-based code generation) or frontier reasoning models as discovery agents would strengthen the generalizability of the benchmark findings.

High Failure Rates on DiscoBench All: On tasks where all modules are editable simultaneously, the agent success rates drop dramatically (11.4% to 34.3%), driven frequently by basic syntax errors or hardcoded tensor shapes. While this demonstrates ample headroom, the sparsity of successful runs leads to wide confidence intervals and high variance in Elo ratings for the 'All' setting.

Scope of ADA Optimization Case Study: While the prompt optimization experiment is illustrative, it is restricted to 30 steps of text-based meta-prompt updates using Claude-4.5 Sonnet. Exploring model weight optimization (e.g., reinforcement learning or fine-tuning from discovery trajectories, as proposed in Section 6.2) remains entirely future work.
